notes.short: A saying: “Do we not all have one Father?”
notes.about: Malachi asks a question that, first found here, later passed into use as a saying: “Do we not all have one Father?” He turns it on the people: if they share one Father, why do they break faith with one another? Later, some made the same appeal when arguing with Jesus (John 8:33, 39, 41).

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: Do we not all have one Father?
figure.means: a saying that all Israel shared one Father, which the prophet turns against their breaking faith with one another

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the question under Parœmia, among sayings that first appear in Scripture and have since passed into general use, and says the Jews used this proverb in their controversy with the Lord in John 8:33 and 8:39. The verse itself applies it to their breaking faith with one another.
notes.limit: The verse itself does not mark the question as a proverb.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 763
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “Have we not all one father?” The Jews used this proverb in their controversy with the Lord in Joh 8:33 ; Joh 8:39 , etc.
